learningObjectives.title: Uses and dangers of EM waves

questions.q: Why does light bend (refract) when it passes from air into glass?
options: Its speed changes, which changes its direction (unless it hits the boundary along the normal)
It speeds up in the glass
questions.explain: Refraction happens because the wave changes speed when it enters a different medium. Light slows down in glass; if it meets the boundary at an angle, this change of speed bends it toward the normal.

questions.q: Which list shows the electromagnetic spectrum in order of INCREASING frequency?
options: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
Gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
Radio, visible, microwave, X-ray, infrared, gamma, ultraviolet
Microwave, radio, infrared, visible, gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet
questions.explain: In order of increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength): radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Gamma rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength.

questions.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used for broadcasting television and radio signals over long distances?
questions.explain: Radio waves are used for TV and radio broadcasting. They have long wavelengths and can be transmitted, received and reflected over long distances.

questions.q: Which use is correctly matched to the EM wave?
options: Microwaves – cooking food and satellite communications
questions.explain: Microwaves are used for cooking and satellite/mobile communications. Infrared is used in remote controls and heating; gamma rays sterilise equipment and treat cancer; UV causes tanning.

questions.q: When a wave is reflected from a flat surface, how does the angle of reflection compare with the angle of incidence (both measured from the normal)?
options: The angle of reflection is larger
The angle of reflection is smaller
The wave is absorbed, not reflected
questions.explain: For reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal to the surface.

questions.q: How do all electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum?
options: At different speeds depending on frequency
All at the same speed (the speed of light)
They cannot travel through a vacuum
Only visible light can travel through a vacuum
questions.explain: All EM waves are transverse and travel at the same speed (about 3 × 10⁸ m/s) through a vacuum. They differ in frequency and wavelength, not speed in a vacuum.

questions.q: Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays can be dangerous to living cells mainly because they are:
options: Ionising, so they can damage cells and DNA and cause cancer
Too slow to escape the body
questions.explain: UV, X-rays and gamma rays carry high energy and are ionising. They can damage cells and mutate DNA, increasing the risk of cancer; radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv).

questions.q: Compared with radio waves, gamma rays have a:
questions.explain: Gamma rays sit at the high-frequency end of the spectrum, so they have a much shorter wavelength and higher frequency than radio waves (frequency and wavelength are inversely related for a fixed speed).

questions.q: Which EM wave is used in fibre-optic communications and in TV remote controls?
questions.explain: Infrared is used to carry signals along optical fibres and in remote controls. It is also emitted by warm objects and used in thermal imaging.

questions.q: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from glass towards air and the angle of incidence is:
options: Equal to the angle of refraction
questions.explain: When light goes from a denser to a less dense medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, all the light is reflected back inside — this is total internal reflection.

questions.q: Total internal reflection is used to carry light along optical fibres. Which other application relies on it?
options: An endoscope used to see inside the body
questions.explain: Endoscopes and optical fibres use total internal reflection to guide light (and images) along curved fibres without it escaping the sides.

questions.q: When light passes from glass into air (along a line not on the normal), it bends:
options: Towards the normal because it slows down
Away from the normal because it speeds up
It does not bend at all
questions.explain: Light speeds up when it enters a less dense medium (glass to air), so it refracts away from the normal.

questions.q: Which EM wave is used in medical X-ray imaging of bones?
questions.explain: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by denser bone, producing a shadow image. They are ionising, so doses are kept low and staff are shielded.

questions.q: Spending too long in strong sunlight can damage skin. Which EM radiation from the Sun is mainly responsible for sunburn and skin cancer?
questions.explain: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is ionising enough to damage skin cells and DNA, causing sunburn, premature ageing and an increased risk of skin cancer.

questions.q: Which use is correctly matched to its EM wave?
options: Infrared – thermal imaging cameras and heating
questions.explain: Infrared is emitted by warm objects and is used in thermal imaging and heaters. Gamma rays (not microwaves) treat cancer; microwaves carry phone/satellite signals; remotes use infrared, not X-rays.

questions.q: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.explain: Within the visible spectrum, red light has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency, while violet has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency.

questions.q: A red book looks red in white light because it:
options: Absorbs red light and reflects all other colours
Reflects red light and absorbs the other colours
questions.explain: An opaque coloured object reflects the colours we see and absorbs the rest. A red book reflects red light and absorbs the other colours of white light.

questions.q: A surface that scatters light in many directions, rather than forming a clear image, produces:
questions.explain: A rough surface causes diffuse reflection: the normals point in many directions so reflected rays scatter. A smooth surface gives specular reflection and a clear image.
